newsitem.title: MONACO: TENNIS-MOYA LINES UP SEMIFINAL AGAINST RIOS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-MOYA LINES UP SEMIFINAL AGAINST RIOS.

text.p: Australian Open finalist Carlos Moya led the Spanish charge at the Monte Carlo tennis Open on Friday, beating Wimbledon champion Richard Krajicek to line up an appetising semifinal against Chile's Marcelo Rios.

The Spaniard, seeded sixth, changed pace early in the second set of his quarter-final clash with the Dutchman to win 1-6 6-2 6-4 and qualify for his second consecutive semifinal on clay after Barcelona last week.

Seventh seeded Rios eased past Sweden's Magnus Larsson 6-1 6-2 to reach his second consecutive semifinal here. Since the start of the tournament, the 21-year-old Chilean has been the most impressive player.
"I play pretty good. Did not make unforced errors. Played my game," said Rios, usually as dull in interviews as he is brilliant on court.
"I've never played Moya. I think it's going to be a tough match."
Moya will be one of two Spaniards in the last four. Compatriot Alex Corretja, seeded 12th, crushed Norwegian qualifier Christian Ruud 6-2 6-0.
But the Spanish presence is still not as impressive as in recent weeks when there were four of them in the semifinals in both Estoril and Barcelona, the two previous European claycourt tournaments.

Frenchman Fabrice Santoro prevented qualifier Carlos Costa from joining his compatriots in the last four. Santoro, who beat claycourt kings Thomas Muster and Sergi Bruguera in the previous rounds, won 6-3 7-5.
He will meet Corretja in the semifinal, hoping to reach his first ATP Tour final since 1994.

"I slowed my serve a little bit at the start of the second set because trying to hit too hard in the first set I realised I was giving him chances to go to the net," said Moya, whose serve has been recorded at 214 kph.

"It's useless on clay. You just need a different mentality," added Moya, the sixth seed, who has ironically achieved his best results on hardcourt despite being bred on the slow surface like most Spaniards.

Krajicek is not a claycourt specialist, despite reaching the French Open semifinals in 1993, and it showed on Friday as he relied much too heavily on his serve and volley game and was far too impatient.
"I'm not afraid of anybody on clay," he said.
"But physically I was not in good shape. I felt a little bit sleepy. I was just tired and I was rushing too much to finish points," said the Dutchman who won in Tokyo on hardcourt last week.
"It's just tough to play on clay. It takes a little bit of time to move the right way."
The tournament's fourth seed also complained about spectators who have lunch outside above central court and talk loudly regardless of the match taking place below.
"It's just rude. Telephones go off. It's a joke sometimes. They should show a little respect for the players and I regret they just don't," he said.
